title: Chapter 47: The Beguiling Boy 2
content:
Chapter 47

The Beguiling Boy 2

The date for the grand Discussion Conference at Koi Tower arrived in the blink of an eye.

While most major cultivation clans planted their ancestral residences on secluded peaks tucked away in nature, the Lanling Jin Sect had staked their claim right in the bustling heart of Lanling City. The primary route to the summit was a paved carriage ramp stretching nearly two miles uphill, opened exclusively for lavish banquets and major conferences. Sect protocol strictly forbade rushing along the slope. Lining both sides of the drive were richly colored bas-reliefs detailing the glorious exploits of previous Jin clan leaders and notable figures, while an attendant driving the carriage offered casual commentary on the historical highlights.

Naturally, the current sect leader, Jin Guangyao, took up four of the most prominent panels: Passing Secrets, The Ambush, The Sworn Brotherhood, and Favor and Might. They illustrated his underground intelligence gathering during the Sunshot Campaign, his assassination of Wen Ruohan, the legendary oath between the Three Zuns, and his enforcement of the Chief Cultivator’s decrees. The artist possessed a rare eye for detail; at a glance, the paintings were merely skillful, but a closer look revealed something unnerving. Even in the panel where he was driving a blade into someone’s back with fresh blood splattered across his cheek, Jin Guangyao’s eyes were delicately crinkled with warm, gentle laughter, sending a subtle chill down the viewer's spine.

Directly following Jin Guangyao's panels were those of Jin Zixuan. Usually, to cement absolute supremacy, a reigning sect leader would deliberately cut down the murals honoring their generation's peers or quietly hire a lesser artisan to ensure they weren't outshined—a petty bit of ego everyone in the cultivation world quietly overlooked. Yet Jin Zixuan occupied four whole murals as well, sharing equal prestige with the man currently running the sect. In the painting, the handsome young master stood radiant with pride, brimming with unrestrained arrogance. Stepping down from the carriage, Wei Wuxian lingered before the wall, staring up at it in silence. Beside him, Lan Wangji halted, waiting without a word.

Not far ahead, a disciple announced, "Gusu Lan Sect, please proceed through this gate."

"Let us go," Lan Wangji said quietly.

Wei Wuxian nodded, stepping alongside him.

The summit opened up into an immense courtyard paved with finely polished flagstones, swarming with guests. The Lanling Jin Sect had clearly expanded and renovated the grounds multiple times over the intervening years; the sheer ostentatious luxury far eclipsed what Wei Wuxian remembered from his past life. In the distance, a tiered staircase supported a colossal white jade Sumeru plinth. Above it sat a magnificent palace beneath double-eaved hip-and-gable roofs, looking down over a vast, roaring sea of Sparks Amidst Snow peonies.

Sparks Amidst Snow was the famed crest of the Lanling Jin Clan—a rare, prized white peony. The petals bloomed in two distinct layers: an outer ring of broad, snow-white petals rolling like frozen waves, cradling an inner blossom of slender, delicate filaments crowned with shimmering golden pollen that caught the sun like glittering stardust. A single blossom was a sight of unmatched splendor; tens of thousands blooming in unison created a spectacle that beggared description.

Several wide avenues branched across the plaza, ushering the arriving delegations forward in crisp, orderly succession:

"Moling Su Sect, please enter here."

"Qinghe Nie Sect, please enter here."

"Yunmeng Jiang Sect, please enter here."

The second Jiang Cheng showed his face, his gaze sharpened into twin daggers. He strode over, his tone flat and unreadable. "Ze-wu-jun. Hanguang-jun."

Lan Xichen inclined his head politely. "Sect Leader Jiang."

With both of their minds elsewhere, the pleasantries were paper-thin. Jiang Cheng asked, "I don't recall seeing Hanguang-jun attend the conferences at Koi Tower in recent years. What inspired the sudden change of heart?"

Neither of the Twin Jades offered an answer, but Jiang Cheng hadn't genuinely cared for one anyway. His gaze had already slid over to Wei Wuxian, his tone dripping with enough venom to run a flying sword through him. "I was under the impression the two of you never dragged stray freeloaders to formal diplomatic visits. What brought on this miracle? Just who is this distinguished cultivator? Might you introduce us?"

Right on cue, a warm, smiling voice cut through the tension: "Second Brother, why didn't you give me a heads-up that Wangji was tagging along?"

The master of Koi Tower himself, Lianfang-zun Jin Guangyao, stepped forward to welcome them personally.

Lan Xichen returned the smile, Lan Wangji offered a formal bow, and Wei Wuxian quietly took the measure of the man reigning as Chief Cultivator.

Jin Guangyao possessed a remarkably advantageous face. His complexion was fair, accented by a neat vermilion dot between his brows. His dark eyes were bright and quick, alert without feeling slippery, framed by sharp, handsome features that carried a soft, disarming charm. A perpetual, gentle curve graced his lips and brow, making him look thoroughly approachable and harmless. It was the kind of face that easily won over women without putting men on guard; elders found him endearing, while juniors found him warm and trustworthy. Even if you didn't particularly care for him, it was near impossible to actively despise him—truly an enormous social advantage. Though on the shorter side, his poised carriage more than made up for it. Dressed in the ceremonial robes of his clan beneath a black gauze gauze cap, a blooming white peony embroidered over his heart and a jade-ring sash at his waist, his hand rested heavily against his sword hilt—radiating an unmistakable, quiet authority.

Jin Ling had trailed out right behind him. Still too chicken to face Jiang Cheng alone, he hid behind Jin Guangyao’s hem, offering a weak mumble: "Uncle."

Jiang Cheng barked, "Oh, so you still remember I'm your uncle?!"

Jin Ling gave Jin Guangyao's robes a frantic tug. Jin Guangyao, a man seemingly born to smooth over rough edges, chuckled softly. "Come now, Sect Leader Jiang. A-Ling has been beating himself up for days; he's been so terrified of your temper he barely touched a bowl of rice. Boys will be reckless—you dote on him more than anyone, so don't be too hard on him."

Jin Ling chimed in at lightning speed, "Right, right! Youngest Uncle can vouch for me—I haven't had an appetite all week!"

Jiang Cheng sneered, "Lost your appetite? With color that flush in your cheeks, you haven't missed a single meal!"

Before Jin Ling could talk back, his eyes snagged on Wei Wuxian lingering behind Lan Wangji. His jaw dropped, blurted out before he could catch himself: "What the hell are you doing here?!"

Wei Wuxian shrugged cheerfully. "Crashing for the free food."

Jin Ling bristled, his temper flaring. "You actually dared show your face?! Didn't I warn—"

Jin Guangyao reached back, ruffling Jin Ling’s hair and gently steering him behind his robes with a chuckle. "Now, now. A guest is a guest. Koi Tower might run short on many things, but we certainly have enough food to go around." Turning back to Lan Xichen, he said, "Second Brother, please, take your seats inside while I see to the reception out here. I’ll have the servants set up a proper table for Wangji right away."

Lan Xichen nodded. "Do not go out of your way on our account."

"How is it out of the way?" Jin Guangyao scolded gently. "You're family here—stop standing on ceremony."

If Jin Guangyao had met a person even once, he could permanently recall their face, name, title, and age, greeting them warmly with effortless familiarity even decades later. If he’d crossed paths with them twice, he committed every single one of their personal quirks, likes, and dislikes to memory, flawlessly catering to their preferences while sidestepping their pet peeves. Since Lan Wangji’s attendance had been completely unannounced, no seat had been assigned to him; Jin Guangyao immediately bustled off to fix the oversight.

Filing into the Glamour Hall, the guests strolled down lush crimson carpets. Stationed along both sides by the dark sandalwood tables were stunning maidens in kingfisher-feather hairpins, greeting the arrivals with refined smiles. Every girl possessed a lithe waist and an elegant poise, uniform in height and grace to create a seamless, harmonious aesthetic. Wei Wuxian had never been able to resist appreciating pretty women; settling into his seat, he flashed a charming grin at the attendant pouring his wine. "Much obliged."

The girl jumped slightly, fluttering her eyelashes as her gaze darted away in visible panic. Wei Wuxian blinked in confusion before catching on, casting a casual glance across the room. Sure enough, weird stares were burning into him from all directions—nearly half the Jin Clan disciples were eyeing him like an unwelcome ghost.

He’d almost forgotten: this was Koi Tower, the very place where Mo Xuanyu had been publicly disgraced and kicked out for harassing his fellow disciples. Who could have imagined he’d swagger right back in, shamelessly perched among the premier seats alongside the Twin Jades of Lan...

Wei Wuxian leaned sideways toward Lan Wangji, keeping his voice to a whisper. "Hanguang-jun. Hanguang-jun."

"What?"

"Don't you dare wander off and leave me alone," Wei Wuxian murmured. "Half this room probably knows Mo Xuanyu by face. If someone comes over to catch up on old times, I'll have no choice but to start raving like a lunatic again. If I end up embarrassing you, don't blame me."

Lan Wangji cast an unreadable look his way. "So long as you do not go out of your way to provoke them."

Just then, Jin Guangyao reentered the hall, escorting an elegantly draped lady at his side. Though her deportment was graceful and dignified, an air of youthful innocence clung to her delicate features. It was the mistress of Koi Tower, Jin Guangyao’s legal wife, Qin Su.

For years, the pair had been held up as the golden standard of marital devotion across the cultivation world—treating each other with unyielding mutual respect. Qin Su hailed from the Qin Clan of Laoling, a subsidiary branch of Lanling Jin, where her father Qin Cangye had been a fiercely loyal veteran serving Jin Guangshan for decades. Though Jin Guangyao was technically a sect leader's son, his mother's background meant their marriage was socially asymmetrical on paper. Yet during the Sunshot Campaign, Jin Guangyao had personally saved Qin Su’s life. Utterly devoted, she had stood by him through thick and thin, adamantly refusing anyone else until their union became the stuff of romantic legend. And Jin Guangyao had never failed her. Despite holding absolute dominion as Chief Cultivator, his personal life was night and day compared to his lecherous father: he never took concubines, nor had he ever strayed an inch with another woman—an absolute fidelity that left many clan mistresses burning with envy.

Watching Jin Guangyao hold his wife's hand, escorting her with doting care while hovering to make sure she didn't trip over the jade steps, Wei Wuxian thought the rumors weren't exaggerated in the slightest.

Once the couple took the head seats, the banquet officially commenced. Seated right below them was Jin Ling, puffing out his chest, throwing relentless, venomous glares across the aisle at Wei Wuxian. Accustomed to being gawked at his entire life, Wei Wuxian ate and drank in complete bliss, tuning out the sea of flattering toasts filling the hall.

By the time the feast concluded, night had settled in. With the formal debates slated for the following morning, the guests trickled out in scattered groups, guided toward their guest chambers by attendant disciples. Noticing Lan Xichen looked unusually weighed down by brooding thoughts, Jin Guangyao stepped forward, calling softly, "Second Brother—"

Before he could finish, a panicked figure barreled into his chest, howling like a dying animal: "Third Brother!!!"

The impact knocked Jin Guangyao back a step, forcing him to scramble to keep his cap from flying off. "Huaisang, what's happened? Calm down and speak properly."

Across the great clans, the only sect leader who could pull off this level of shameless undignified hysterics was Qinghe Nie’s resident Head-Shaker. And a drunken Head-Shaker was twice the disaster. Red-faced and weeping, Nie Huaisang clutched Jin Guangyao's lapels in a vice grip. "Third Brother!! What am I going to do?! Can you help me just one more time?! I swear this is the absolute last time!!!"

Jin Guangyao sighed helplessly. "Didn't I already dispatch a few hands to settle that matter for you?"

Nie Huaisang wailed at the top of his lungs, "That one was settled, but a whole new disaster just popped up! Third Brother, what am I going to do?! I want to die!"

Realizing the man wasn't going to spit out a coherent sentence anytime soon, Jin Guangyao turned back to his wife. "A-Su, head back to our quarters first. Huaisang, come along, let's find a quiet room to talk this through. Stop panicking..."

As he steered the weeping mess away, Lan Xichen moved to check on them, only to be dragged into the huddle by the drunken Nie Huaisang as well.

Qin Su offered Lan Wangji a polite curtsy. "Hanguang-jun, it has been many years since you last graced our conferences. If our hospitality falls short in any way, please pardon the oversight."

Her voice was soft and sweet, carrying a gentle grace that naturally invited warmth. Lan Wangji dipped his head in return. Her gaze lingered on Wei Wuxian for an awkward, hesitant beat before she murmured, "Please excuse me," slipping away with her maidservants.

Wei Wuxian scratched his cheek. "Why is everyone on this mountain looking at me like I'm a three-headed freak? What did Mo Xuanyu actually do? Make a public pass at someone? So what? The Jin Clan really needs to get out more."

Lan Wangji offered a subtle shake of his head at his rambling.

Wei Wuxian added, "I'm going to fish around for some gossip. Keep an eye on Jiang Cheng for me, will you? If he doesn't look for me, great; if he does, run interference."

"Do not wander far," Lan Wangji murmured.

Wei Wuxian grinned. "Understood. If I get lost, I'll see you in our room tonight."

Scanning the courtyard, he didn't spot his intended target. Leaving Lan Wangji’s side, he wandered past an ornamental pavilion when a sharp hiss cut through the rockery: "Hey!"

Wei Wuxian smiled. Bingo.

Turning around, he drawled, "What's with the 'hey'? Where are your manners? Weren't we getting along famously when we parted ways? So cold the second we meet again—you're breaking my heart."

Jin Ling broke out in a full-body shudder. "Shut your mouth! Who got along with you?! Didn't I warn you ages ago to stop hanging around my family? Why the hell did you come back?!"

Wei Wuxian held his hands up in faux innocence. "Heaven is my witness, I've been glued to Hanguang-jun's side this whole time—I might as well have asked him to leash me! Where did you see me bothering your family? Hitting on your uncle? He's the one who won't stop hounding me!"

Jin Ling snapped, "Shut up! My uncle only suspects you! Stop running your mouth—don't think I don't know you still harbor filthy designs on—"

A chorus of arrogant shouts cut him off as seven or eight teenage disciples in Jin gold leapt down from the garden paths, surrounding them. Jin Ling’s jaw clamped shut.

Leading the pack was a youth roughly Jin Ling's age, though built noticeably stockier. "I thought my eyes were playing tricks on me," he sneered. "It really is him."

Wei Wuxian pointed at his own chest. "Me?"

"Who else?! Mo Xuanyu, you actually had the shameless audacity to crawl back?"

Jin Ling frowned. "Jin Chan, what are you doing here? This is none of your business."

Ah, Wei Wuxian realized. A peer from the clan—and clearly a rival pack.

Jin Chan scoffed, "If it's none of my business, it's none of yours either! Who are you to tell me what to do?"

At a flick of his wrist, three or four boys moved forward to pin Wei Wuxian down. Jin Ling sidestepped instantly, planting himself squarely in front of him. "Don't touch him!"

Jin Chan sneered, "What's the matter, Jin Ling? What's wrong with teaching an undisciplined disciple of our house a lesson?"

"Wake up!" Jin Ling spat. "He was kicked to the curb ages ago! He isn't a disciple of our clan anymore!"

"So what?"

The sheer, shameless arrogance of that retort left Wei Wuxian thoroughly entertained.

Jin Ling fired back, "So what? Did you forget whose company he arrived with today? You want to rough him up? Why don't you go ask Hanguang-jun's permission first?"

The name Hanguang-jun acted like an instant freezing charm, every boy shrinking back with nervous twitches. Even with Lan Wangji nowhere in sight, none of them had the suicidal guts to claim they weren't terrified of him.

After an awkward beat, Jin Chan sneered, "Heh. Jin Ling, weren't you the one who hated his guts the most? Why the sudden change of heart?"

"What's with all the lip?" Jin Ling bristled. "Whether I hate him or not is none of your damn business!"

Jin Chan’s voice dropped into a greasy scoff. "The bastard shamelessly threw himself at Lianfang-zun, and you're still defending him?"

A bolt of lightning seemed to rip straight through Wei Wuxian’s skull.

Threw himself at who?

Lianfang-zun?

Jin Guangyao?!

The male disciple Mo Xuanyu had supposedly harassed... was the Chief Cultivator himself?!

Before he could pull his brain out of the gutter, Jin Ling and Jin Chan had already traded enough insults to blow the lid off.

"You want a brawl? Let's go!" Jin Ling barked.

A boy in the back jeered, "Come on then! Everyone knows you can't fight without running to your mutt for help!"

Jin Ling’s hand had been drifting toward his whistle, but the taunt made him grit his teeth so hard they nearly cracked. "I don't need Fairy to beat the snot out of the lot of you!!!"

His roar carried plenty of spirit, but taking on eight boys alone was a fool's errand. Before long, Jin Ling was driven backward, stumbling straight into Wei Wuxian's chest. Seeing him just lounging there, Jin Ling snapped, "What are you standing around for?!"

Wei Wuxian’s hand shot out, clamping around Jin Ling’s wrist. Before the boy could even shout, an irresistible force twisted through his joint, throwing him flat onto his knees in the dirt.

Jin Ling shrieked in fury, "Are you suicidal?!"

Watching him flip the very boy defending him caught Jin Chan and his cronies flat-footed.

Wei Wuxian looked down calmly. "Catch that?"

Jin Ling blinked through the dirt. "What?"

Wei Wuxian twisted his fingers again. "Did you learn it?"

A sharp, numbing ache shot up Jin Ling’s arm, pulling another yelp from his throat—yet his mind instantly replayed the microscopic, lightning-fast flick Wei Wuxian had just executed.

"Watch close this time," Wei Wuxian instructed.

A boy charged forward to exploit the opening. Keeping one hand casually tucked behind his back, Wei Wuxian’s free fingers caught the oncoming wrist, effortlessly sending the attacker face-planting into the flagstones in the blink of an eye.

This time, Jin Ling saw every single angle. The lingering ache in his own wrist showed him precisely which acupoint to flood with spiritual energy. Bounding to his feet, eyes blazing, he roared, "Got it!"

The tide flipped in an instant. Within minutes, the garden echoed with panicked shrieks and bruised curses as Jin Ling flipped his attackers like flapjacks.

Scrambling to retreat down the path, Jin Chan howled, "Jin Ling, you just wait!"

The gang fled in disgrace, leaving Jin Ling throwing his head back in wild, triumphant laughter.

Once he’d caught his breath, Wei Wuxian asked, "First time winning a brawl?"

Jin Ling spat. "Bah! One-on-one, I've never lost a fight in my life! But Jin Chan always brings a mob like a coward."

Wei Wuxian nearly told him that he could just bring his own mob—street brawls were about numbers, not noble honor—but remembered that Jin Ling was always alone on his hunts, lacking any peers his age to back him up. He swallowed the words.

Jin Ling looked over. "Hey. Where did you learn that trick?"

Without a shred of shame, Wei Wuxian tossed the credit straight onto his companion. "Hanguang-jun taught me."

Having seen Lan Wangji's ribbon tied around his wrists with his own two eyes, Jin Ling bought it without hesitation, muttering, "He actually teaches you parlor tricks?"

"Naturally. But it's just a quick stunt; it only worked because they'd never seen it before. Use it too often and people adapt. Want to learn a few more?"

Jin Ling looked at him, murmuring, "What's wrong with you? My youngest uncle always tells me to keep the peace, yet here you are egging me on."

"Tells you what?" Wei Wuxian asked. "Don't fight, play nice with others?"

"Pretty much."

"Don't listen to him," Wei Wuxian scoffed. "Let me tell you: when you grow up, you'll find there are a hundred more people you want to punch in the mouth, but you'll have to force yourself to smile and play nice with every single one of them. While you're still young, fight whoever you want and have a blast! If you don't get into a few spectacular brawls at your age, your youth is an absolute waste."

A flicker of yearning crossed Jin Ling's eyes, though he kept up his defensive front. "Nonsense. My uncle has my best interests at heart." Then, a thought struck him: the old Mo Xuanyu had practically worshiped Jin Guangyao like a divine icon, never daring to question a word he said. Telling him to ignore his uncle... did that mean he was truly over his obsession?

Reading his mind like an open book, Wei Wuxian decided to lay it on thick. "Looks like the cat's out of the bag. You caught me: my heart belongs to someone else now."

Jin Ling stared, speechless.

Wei Wuxian clasped his hands over his chest with theatrical passion. "During my time away, I did some deep soul-searching. I finally realized Lianfang-zun simply isn't my type, nor is he right for me."

Jin Ling took two nervous steps back.

Wei Wuxian pressed forward, eyes shimmering with mock fervor. "I was blind to my own feelings before, but meeting Hanguang-jun changed everything." He drew in a dramatic, trembling breath. "I can't live without him now. I don't want anyone in this world except my Hanguang-jun—hey, where are you running?! I wasn't finished! Jin Ling! Jin Ling!"

Jin Ling had spun on his heel and bolted like his pants were on fire, refusing to look back no matter how loud Wei Wuxian yelled.

Wei Wuxian chuckled smugly to himself. Well, that settles that. The kid definitely won't think I'm eyeing Jin Guangyao anymore.

Turning around with a smirk, the breath died in his throat.

Standing barely ten paces away under the pale moonlight was a pristine figure in white, watching him with an entirely unreadable, tranquil gaze.

Lan Wangji.

Wei Wuxian froze.

Back when he’d first returned to the living world, he wouldn't have blinked an eye delivering a monologue ten times more shameless right to Lan Wangji's face. Yet caught red-handed right now, a bizarre, unprecedented wave of genuine embarrassment prickled up his neck—a sensation he hadn't felt in two lifetimes.

Shoving the embarrassment down with practiced ease, he sauntered over with an airy laugh. "Hanguang-jun, you're back! Did you know Mo Xuanyu was kicked off Koi Tower for chasing after Jin Guangyao? No wonder everyone was looking at me like I was radioactive!"

Lan Wangji said nothing, falling into step beside him.

Wei Wuxian mused, "Since neither you nor Ze-wu-jun knew about it, the Jin clan clearly buried the scandal under the rug. It makes sense, really: Mo Xuanyu carried clan blood. If Jin Guangshan didn't want him, he wouldn't have brought him home in the first place. Merely bothering an ordinary disciple would've earned him a beating at most, not banishment. But hitting on Jin Guangyao? Not only was he Lianfang-zun, he was his own half-brother. What an absolute mess..."

It was a stain that had to be severed at the roots, and since nobody could touch the Chief Cultivator, Mo Xuanyu had taken the fall.

Recalling Jin Guangyao's effortless warmth earlier—acting as though he barely registered the guest—Wei Wuxian couldn't help but admire the man's terrifying poker face. Jin Ling, on the other hand, had zero subtlety; his deep disgust for Mo Xuanyu wasn't just a hatred of cutsleeves, but burning fury over someone targeting his beloved youngest uncle.

Thinking of the boy, Wei Wuxian let out a quiet sigh.

"What is it?" Lan Wangji asked softly.

"Hanguang-jun, have you noticed that every time Jin Ling goes out on a night-hunt, he's always alone?" Wei Wuxian said. "Don't count Jiang Cheng—his uncle doesn't count. A teenager with no peers his age flanking him? When we were young..." Catching the faint arch of Lan Wangji's brow, Wei Wuxian quickly corrected himself: "Right, me. When I was young. I certainly never ran solo."

Lan Wangji’s voice was calm. "That was you. Not everyone is like you."

"Sure, but kids naturally crave crowds and noise," Wei Wuxian countered. "Do you think Jin Ling is simply that isolated? Not a single friend in his own clan? Forget the Jiang Clan for a second; among the Jin juniors, not a single one gets along with him—they were just brawling in the dirt. Doesn't Jin Guangyao have any children around his age?"

"Jin Guangyao once had a son," Lan Wangji murmured. "He was murdered in his youth."

Wei Wuxian blinked. "The young heir of Koi Tower? Who could manage to murder him?"

"The Watchtowers."

"Explain."

As it turned out, Jin Guangyao’s push to erect the Watchtowers had earned him countless bitter political enemies. When one dissenting sect leader lost the ideological debate, malice festered until he ruthlessly assassinated Jin Guangyao and Qin Su’s only child. The boy had been sweet and gentle, deeply adored by both parents. In a wave of icy fury, Jin Guangyao had eradicated the entire offending clan root and branch in retribution. But the trauma shattered Qin Su's health, and she had never conceived again.

Wei Wuxian fell quiet for a moment before shaking his head. "With a temper like Jin Ling's—opening his mouth to offend everyone, throwing punches at the slightest spark—your Jingyi calling him 'Young Mistress' wasn't off the mark. If you and I hadn't stepped in during those past encounters, he’d have gotten himself killed three times over. Jiang Cheng has no clue how to raise a kid, and as for Jin Guangyao..."

Remembering their real objective at Koi Tower, a dull ache throbbed in Wei Wuxian's temples. Lan Wangji watched him in silence, offering no empty platitudes, but listening intently to every word.

Wei Wuxian rubbed his face. "Never mind. Let's head back to the room."

Their assigned guest quarters were sprawling and lavish, furnished with a polished table holding a delicate set of white porcelain wine cups. Wei Wuxian idled by the table, turning a cup in his fingers, waiting until the dead of night before making his move.

Rummaging through the drawers, he procured a stack of blank paper and a pair of shears, quickly cutting out a small paper figurine. It was barely the length of an adult finger, with a round little head and sleeves cut wide like butterfly wings. Dipping a brush in ink, he slashed a few talismanic strokes across the paper, tossed the brush aside, knocked back a mouthful of wine, and collapsed flat onto the mattress.

The paper effigy shuddered. Fluttering its broad sleeves like wings, the weightless scrap took flight, drifting gently through the air until it landed softly on Lan Wangji’s shoulder.

Lan Wangji tilted his head to look. The little paper man immediately scampered up his cheek, scurrying straight onto his forehead ribbon, affectionately tugging and petting the embroidered clouds as if it were the finest treasure on earth. Lan Wangji let the paper spirit fuss over his ribbon for several long seconds before raising a hand to pluck it away. Seeing the incoming fingers, the paper man slid down his nose, its little head bumping—whether by accident or design—right against Lan Wangji’s lips.

Lan Wangji’s fingers froze for a fraction of a heartbeat before gently pinching the paper between two fingers. "Behave."

The little paper man melted limply, curling its flat body snugly around his slender finger.

Lan Wangji’s voice softened. "Be careful on this excursion."

The paper man nodded eagerly, flapped its wings, and flattened itself paper-thin against the floorboards, squeezing through the crack beneath the door to ghost out into the compound.

Koi Tower was locked down tight; a living man had zero hope of slipping past the patrols, but Wei Wuxian had mastered an unorthodox art in his past life: Paper Effigy Divination.

It was exceptionally handy, but carried terrifying risks. It operated on a strict spiritual timer, and the paper body had to return to the host completely intact. If the paper were torn, burned, or destroyed while his consciousness was tethered to it, his soul would suffer identical damage—ranging from slipping into a coma for months to permanent brain damage.

Piloting the tiny scrap, Wei Wuxian hitched a ride under a passing cultivator's hem, slipped beneath door cracks, and fluttered through the night sky disguised as a scrap of drifting trash or a fluttering moth, surveying the sprawling grounds from above.

Suddenly, faint weeping drifted up through the dark. Peeking downward, he spotted one of Jin Guangyao’s private pavilions—the Fragrance Pavilion.

Flitting under the eaves, Wei Wuxian peeked into the reception hall and saw three figures seated together. Nie Huaisang had a desperate grip on Lan Xichen with one hand and Jin Guangyao with the other, utterly sloshed and bawling about god-knows-what. Tucked behind the parlor was a private study; seeing it empty, Wei Wuxian slipped inside for a look. The desk was covered in architectural blueprints annotated with scarlet ink, while the four walls showcased hanging scrolls of the four seasons. He hadn’t planned on lingering, but a single glance pulled a gasp of admiration right out of him. The brushwork and color palette were delicate and serene, yet the compositions possessed a sweeping, boundless depth. A single landscape on paper seemed to hold ten thousand rivers and mountains. Wei Wuxian thought this level of artistry could easily stand shoulder-to-shoulder with Lan Xichen’s—and taking a closer look, he realized the seasonal scrolls were indeed painted by Lan Xichen himself.

Fluttering out of the Zhan Garden, Wei Wuxian spotted an expansive, five-ridged palace in the distance. Its roof gleamed with dazzling golden-glazed tiles, ringed by thirty-two magnificent gilded pillars. That had to be one of the most heavily fortified sanctums on all of Koi Tower: the Fragrance Hall, private chambers of the Lanling Jin Sect leaders throughout history.

Aside from patrols of cultivators clad in Sparks Amidst Snow robes, Wei Wuxian could feel the air and ground humming with a dense, suffocating lattice of warding arrays. He drifted down beside the carved base of a gilded pillar to catch his breath, then spent several agonizing minutes squeezing his paper-thin body through the crack under the double doors.

Compared to the Zhan Garden, the Fragrance Hall was the quintessential embodiment of Koi Tower: painted rafters, carved beams, and blinding opulence. Inside, layers of silk draperies trailed onto the floorboards, while an auspicious beast-shaped censer on a side table puffed ribbons of orchid-scented smoke—an air of languid, cloying luxury bordering on the decadent.

With Jin Guangyao occupied in the gardens with Lan Xichen and Nie Huaisang, the empty hall made for easy searching. The paper man fluttered around the chamber hunting for anything suspicious, his eye suddenly catching an agate paperweight resting on the desk. Tucked beneath it was a letter.

The seal had already been broken. The envelope bore neither name nor clan crest, but its heft made it obvious it wasn't empty. Flapping his sleeves, he touched down on the desktop, eager to see what was inside. He tugged at the edge of the envelope with both paper hands, hauling with all his might, but the heavy agate weight didn't budge an inch.

His current body was a weightless scrap of paper; shifting a solid hunk of stone was completely out of the question.

Paper-Xian circled the agate slab several times, kicking, shoving, and throwing his weight around, but the thing remained an unyielding mountain. Left with no choice, he backed off to scour the room for other leads. Right then, a side door creaked open a fraction.

Wei Wuxian dropped off the desk in a flash, flattening himself motionless against the shadow of a wooden table leg.

Qin Su stepped into the room. The hall hadn’t been empty after all; she had simply been lingering in the adjoining chamber without making a sound.

The lady of Koi Tower being in her own bedchamber was the most natural thing in the world. Yet right now, she looked like a walking disaster. Her face was ashen, drained of every drop of blood, swaying on her feet as though she’d taken a concussive blow to the chest—having just dragged herself out of a dead faint, on the verge of collapsing all over again.

What happened? Wei Wuxian wondered. She was in high spirits back in the banquet hall.

Qin Su leaned heavily against the doorframe, spacing out for a long while before bracing herself along the wall, inching toward the desk. Staring down at the letter pinned beneath the agate paperweight, her hand trembled outward to pick it up, only to violently recoil. Beneath the flickering candlelight, her lips quivered without pause, her refined, delicate features twisting into an agonizing grimace.

Out of nowhere, a strangled shriek tore from her throat. She snatched the letter from the desk, hurling it to the floor, her other hand clawing convulsively at the silk over her chest. Wei Wuxian’s eyes lit up, but he forced himself to hold back. If only Qin Su spotted him, he could manage an escape; but if her screaming summoned the guards and his paper vessel caught a tear, his tethered soul would take the hit.

A voice cut through the room without warning: "A-Su, what are you doing?"

Qin Su whipped around. Standing just a few paces behind her was that familiar, graceful silhouette, his face wearing its usual, gentle smile.

She scrambled to the floor, scooping the letter into her arms. Pinned behind the desk leg, Wei Wuxian could only watch helplessly as the papers slipped out of his line of sight once more. Jin Guangyao took a quiet step forward. "What is that in your hand?"

His tone was sweet and tender, acting as though he hadn't noticed a single oddity—blind to the strange letter in her grip, blind to her contorted expression—asking with the casual ease of checking if she needed an extra cloak. Qin Su clutched the papers white-knuckled, offering no reply. Jin Guangyao pressed, "You don't look well. What's the matter?"

Dripping with doting concern, his voice only made her tremble harder. Raising the crumpled pages, she choked out, "...I met with someone."

"With whom?"

Ignoring him, she rasped, "This person told me a great deal... and handed me this letter."

Jin Guangyao let out a soft, helpless laugh. "Whoever they were, do you believe everything a stranger tells you?"

"They wouldn't lie to me," she cried. "Never."

Who is this person? Wei Wuxian wondered. The third-person pronoun gave away nothing of their gender.

Qin Su’s voice shook. "The things written here... are they true?"

"A-Su, if you don't let me read it, how am I supposed to know what it says?"

She shoved the sheets toward him. "Fine! Read it!"

Jin Guangyao stepped closer to take the pages. He scanned the lines with terrifying speed, skimming the text in seconds without a single flicker in his expression—not a shadow of guilt crossing his brow.

Qin Su was on the verge of a hysterical shriek. "Say something! Speak! Tell me it's not true! Tell me it's all foul, sickening lies!"

Jin Guangyao’s voice remained firm and comforting. "It isn't true. Every word is a vile fabrication. Baseless slander engineered to frame me."

Qin Su burst into ragged sobs. "Liar! Even now you're lying to my face! I don't believe you!"

Jin Guangyao sighed softly. "A-Su, you begged me to say it. I say it, and you refuse to believe me. What am I supposed to do?"

She flung the letter straight into his chest, burying her face in her hands. "Heavens... Heavens, heavens, heavens! You... you're a monster! How could you?! How could you do this?!"

Choking on her own words, she stumbled back against a wooden pillar, doubled over, and violently dry-heaved.

She retched with gut-wrenching agony, as though trying to heave up her very soul. Watching this visceral revulsion, Wei Wuxian’s paper eyes went wide. She must have been puking her guts out in the back room earlier. What the hell was written in that letter? That he murdered someone and chopped up the corpse? But everyone knows Jin Guangyao spilled oceans of blood during the Sunshot Campaign, and her own father has plenty of blood on his hands. Was it about Mo Xuanyu? No, there’s no way Jin Guangyao actually fooled around with him; ten to one, Mo Xuanyu's banishment was an orchestrated frame-job. Even so, nothing like that warrants this kind of reaction—nauseated to the point of heaving. Though Wei Wuxian didn't know Qin Su well, he’d crossed paths with her in high society. As Qin Cangye’s pampered darling, she was naive and well-bred, never once breaking her pristine composure. Something was dreadfully wrong here.

Listening to her retching, Jin Guangyao quietly crouched down, gathered the scattered sheets from the floor, and touched the corner of the paper to the flame of a bronze lotus lamp. The parchment caught instantly, slowly curling into embers.

Watching the ash drift to the floor, his voice took on a sorrowful tinge. "A-Su, we have been husband and wife for years, living in harmony and mutual respect. As a husband, I have treated you with nothing but devotion. Behaving like this... it truly breaks my heart."

Having nothing left to vomit, Qin Su slumped against the floorboards, weeping miserably. "Treated me well... Yes, you treated me well... But I... I wish I had never laid eyes on you! No wonder ever since... ever since then, you never touched me again... After doing something like that, you should've just slit my throat!"

Jin Guangyao murmured, "A-Su, before you learned of this, were our lives not peaceful? You only feel sick and disgusted because you found out today. It proves this knowledge changes nothing in reality; it causes you no physical harm—it's merely a trick of the mind."

Qin Su shook her head, her face turning an ashen gray. "...Tell me the truth. A-Song... How did A-Song really die?"

Who is A-Song?

Jin Guangyao froze for a second. "A-Song? Why ask me that? You’ve known the truth for years. He was murdered, and I wiped out the clan responsible to avenge our son. Why bring him up out of the blue?"

"I thought I knew," she whispered, her voice hollow. "Now I wonder if every single word I ever believed was a lie."

A look of deep exhaustion washed over Jin Guangyao’s face. "A-Su, what has gotten into you? A-Song was my own flesh and blood. What do you think I did to him? Would you truly place your faith in a faceless coward and an anonymous letter over your own husband?"

Clutching her hair, Qin Su let out an ear-splitting wail. "It's precisely because he was your son that it's horrifying! What did you do to him?! If you were capable of that, what wouldn't you dare do?! And you still expect me to trust you! Gods above!"

"Stop letting your thoughts spiral," Jin Guangyao said, his tone sharpening slightly. "Tell me: who did you meet today? Who handed you that letter?"

She gripped her scalp. "What... what are you going to do to them?"

"If that person could tell you, they can tell the entire world," he said softly. "If they could write one letter, they can write a second, a third, an endless deluge. What do you intend to do? Let this secret be dragged out into the open? A-Su, I am begging you. For the sake of whatever love we shared, tell me: where are the people mentioned in that letter? Who sent you back to read it?"

Who? Wei Wuxian burned to hear the name fall from her lips. Someone capable of approaching the Chief Cultivator’s wife and commanding her absolute trust—someone who held Jin Guangyao's darkest, most unspeakable secret. The contents clearly went far beyond run-of-the-mill murders. It had to be something so deeply grotesque it made Qin Su vomit from pure psychological horror, something so taboo that even behind locked doors with only her husband present, she didn't dare speak the crime aloud. Yet if Qin Su actually surrendered the informant's name, it would be suicide. The moment the words left her mouth, Jin Guangyao wouldn't just hunt down the whistleblower—he’d silence his wife permanently to keep the lid on the grave.

Fortunately, though Qin Su had always been soft, innocent, and perhaps a bit naive, her faith in Jin Guangyao was shattered beyond repair. She stared up at the man sitting so properly by the table—the supreme Chief Cultivator, her husband—who remained immaculate, calm, and striking beneath the candlelight. When he rose and reached down to help her up, Qin Su violently slapped his hand away, collapsing back onto the floorboards with another dry heave.

Jin Guangyao’s brow twitched. "Am I truly that repulsive to you?"

"You're not human," she whispered. "You're a madman!"

A strange, tragic tenderness surfaced in Jin Guangyao’s eyes. "A-Su, back then, I truly had no other path to walk. I intended to carry this secret to my grave, never letting you carry the burden. Now, that informant has ruined everything. If you find me filthy and revolting, so be it; but if this leaks out, you are my legal wife—what do you think the world will say about you? How will they look at you?"

Clutching her head, she shrieked, "Stop talking! Stop reminding me! I wish I had never met you, I wish we had never crossed paths! Why did you pursue me in the first place?!"

After a heavy silence, Jin Guangyao spoke softly. "I know nothing I say now will reach you, but back then, my feelings were entirely genuine."

"Still spinning sweet poison..." she sobbed.

"I speak the truth," he murmured. "I have never forgotten that you never once looked down on my origins or mocked my mother. I have spent my life grateful to you, wanting to cherish, respect, and adore you. But you must understand: even if that enemy hadn't killed A-Song, the boy had to die. He had no choice. If he were allowed to grow up, you and I..."

Mentioning her son shattered her restraint; springing up, she slapped him across the face with all her might. "And whose fault is that?! For this golden throne of yours, is there anything you wouldn't sacrifice?!"

Jin Guangyao didn't flinch, taking the strike square across the cheek, a stark crimson handprint blooming across his fair skin.

He closed his eyes for several seconds. When he opened them, his voice was cool and measured. "A-Su, you truly will not tell me?"

She shook her head weakly. "...Tell you, so you can butcher them too?"

Jin Guangyao sighed. "Listen to yourself. You're delirious with fever. Father-in-law is away traveling for his health; I will arrange for you to join him so you may enjoy family comfort together. Let us wrap this up quickly—there are many guests outside, and the Discussion Conference begins tomorrow."

To care about social decorum and conference politics at a moment like this!

He spoke of sending her away to recuperate, but his hands moved with chilling efficiency, ignoring her thrashing blows to haul her upright. With a subtle flick against her pressure points, Qin Su went entirely limp. With practiced, elegant composure, he half-carried, half-dragged his paralyzed wife through the trailing silk curtains.

Paper-Xian scurried out from beneath the desk, tailing their hems.

Jin Guangyao pressed his palm against a massive, floor-length bronze mirror. A second later, his fingers slipped straight through the polished metal like dipping into water. Qin Su’s eyes were wide with tears, watching in muted horror as her husband dragged her through the looking glass, unable to scream. Knowing the spatial portal would only yield to Jin Guangyao's spiritual signature, Wei Wuxian didn't hesitate—he shot forward and slipped through the seam right on their heels.

Behind the mirror lay a hidden vault. The moment Jin Guangyao stepped inside, wall sconces flared to life on their own, casting an eerie glow over display shelves lining the stone. Shelves held ancient scrolls, leather-bound tomes, rare gems, and spiritual blades. Interspersed among the treasures were various implements of torture: blackened iron rings, barbed spikes, and silver hooks of grotesque, foreign design that radiated sheer dread. Wei Wuxian recognized the craftsmanship instantly—this was Jin Guangyao’s handiwork.

Back during the war, Wen Ruohan had been notoriously sadistic, finding sport in torturing prisoners. Jin Guangyao had secured the tyrant's favor by designing a colorful array of exquisitely brutal torture devices, slowly climbing the ranks until he became Wen Ruohan’s trusted confidant.

Every prominent sect maintained a secret vault or two, so finding one in the Fragrance Hall was hardly a shock.

Aside from a study desk, the chamber housed a long, freezing slab of black iron—sized perfectly for a grown man to lie on. Dark, crusted stains coated the surface. A slaughtering table, Wei Wuxian mused. Ideal for dismemberment.

Jin Guangyao laid Qin Su gently onto the cold metal. Her face was ashen, drained of life. Smoothing a stray lock of hair from her brow, he murmured tenderly, "Do not be afraid. In your state, it is unwise to be seen. With so many guests around, take these few days to rest. The moment you tell me who gave you that letter, you may return to your quarters. If you are willing, simply nod; I did not seal your neck."

Qin Su turned her eyes toward her gentle, doting husband, her gaze brimming with pure horror and despair.

Right then, Wei Wuxian caught sight of a shelf hidden behind a heavy curtain—inscribed with jagged, blood-red runes that radiated an overwhelmingly aggressive binding ward.

Flattening himself against the floorboards, the paper man crept up the stone wall, inch by painstaking inch. Over by the iron slab, Jin Guangyao was still coaxing Qin Su in hushed tones when he suddenly froze, his head snapping around with razor-sharp vigilance.

Aside from him and his paralyzed wife, the vault was dead empty. Jin Guangyao rose, thoroughly inspecting every corner of the chamber. Spotting nothing amiss, he returned to the table.

He had no idea that the instant his neck shifted, Wei Wuxian had already reached a shelf of books. The moment he caught the subtle movement, he slid his paper-thin body between the pages of an open text like a bookmark, his eyes pressed flush against the ink. Fortunately, as paranoid as Jin Guangyao was, it never occurred to him to flip through the library hunting for a flattened human soul.

Pressed against the page, the calligraphy caught Wei Wuxian’s eye. Staring hard at the ink strokes, he cursed internally: No wonder it looks familiar—this is my handwriting!

Jiang Fengmian had once critiqued his brushwork as "reckless and unruly, yet bearing elegant bones." This was undeniably his own hand. Squinting through the dim light, he deciphered phrases: "...distinct from possession..." "...vengeance..." "...forced spiritual pact..." Despite some frayed tears and faded margins, the conclusion was unmistakable: he had sandwiched himself inside his own manuscript. These pages were his personal research notes on the forbidden art of sacrificial summoning, cobbled together from ancient lore and his own theoretical derivations.

Back in his youth, he had scribbled dozens of such manuscripts, tossing them carelessly around his cavern quarters on the Burial Mounds. Some had been reduced to ash during the grand siege, while others—much like his sword—had been looted by the clans as trophies.

The lingering mystery of where Mo Xuanyu had managed to unearth a forbidden ritual finally had an answer.

Knowing this was a volatile, heretical manuscript, Jin Guangyao would never have let an outsider lay eyes on it. It proved that whatever relationship Jin Guangyao and Mo Xuanyu had shared in the past, they had been extraordinarily close.

Jin Guangyao’s voice drifted over: "A-Su, my time is up. I must go host the banquet. I will return to see you later."

Wei Wuxian was just wiggling his way out of the papers when he had to duck back inside. This time, his gaze landed on a different set of documents: two property deeds and land titles.

He found it genuinely bizarre. What was special about ordinary deeds to warrant being locked alongside the Yiling Laozu's forbidden manuscripts? Yet scrutinizing the yellowing parchment, they were completely mundane—no hidden runes, no secret ciphers, just aging paper stained with stray ink. Knowing Jin Guangyao did nothing by accident, Wei Wuxian committed the location to memory: Yunping City in Yunmeng. Perhaps an opportunity would arise to investigate the site later.

Hearing the vault fall quiet, Wei Wuxian resumed his slow crawl along the masonry, finally slipping beneath the warding curtain. Before he could process what sat within the niche, light flooded his vision.

Jin Guangyao had walked over and swept the fabric aside.

For a heartbeat, Wei Wuxian thought his cover was blown. But as the torchlight filtered through the gap, he realized he was cloaked in a deep shadow. A spherical silhouette sat right in front of him, shielding him from view.

Jin Guangyao stood motionless, staring down at the object inside the niche.

After an agonizing silence, he whispered softly:

"Were you looking at me just now?"

Naturally, the room offered no reply. After another beat of silence, Jin Guangyao lowered the curtain.

Wei Wuxian flattened himself against the cold form. It was hard and frozen to the touch, resembling a metal helmet. Drifting around to the front, he was met by an ashen face. To ensure this severed head could neither see, hear, nor speak, the pale skin had been smothered beneath a dense, suffocating lattice of sealing runes, with its eyes, mouth, and ears locked down tight.

Wei Wuxian offered a quiet salute in the dark: Long time no see, Chifeng-zun.
